patch.value: Dependency-kind lexicon: fifteen accepted spellings for roughly eight relations, canonicalized inconsistently at write time, so the stored graph vocabulary keeps fragmenting

The declared dependency-kind domain accepts fifteen spellings, enumerated by the mutation error on an unknown kind (2026.7.25):

  blocks, parent, child, parent_child, child_of, related, related_to, discovered_from, blocked_by, incident_from, epic, implements, supersedes, task, verifies

Those cover roughly eight distinct relations. The hierarchy family alone has five spellings (parent, parent_child, child_of, epic, task) plus the inverse child; the associative family has two (related, related_to). Two of them, epic and task, are item type words used as relationship kinds.

Canonicalization is applied inconsistently. pm-fl0c shipped write-time canonicalization for one alias only: --dep kind=depends_on is stored as blocked_by. Every other alias is stored verbatim. Verified on disk in an isolated sandbox:

  pm-3l9d,child_of,...
  pm-sar6,epic,...
  pm-3l9d,related_to,...

The graph registry then canonicalizes on read: with exactly those three rows on disk, pm graph audit reports edges_by_kind {parent: 2, related: 1}. No edge is lost to graph queries, and this item does not propose changing that read behaviour.

The cost lands on the two consumers that read the store directly. First, the documented composition story: pm data is plain text specifically so agents and operators can drive it with grep and jq, and a pipeline selecting kind == "related" silently misses every related_to row. Second, the native profile hides the fragmentation it is the natural place to surface: edges_by_kind has no related_to key, so an operator cannot see from any command that alias rows exist at all. On the repository tracker there are sixteen related_to rows against 2,189 related rows.

The vocabulary is still growing, so a data-side cleanup alone cannot converge. pm-bwnclq and pm-b1zsk9 were both created on 2026-07-25 carrying related_to rows, and pm-pegcmx carries four from 2026-07-21. pm-p9a4 owns classifying the existing aliases and pm-hnc9w7 owns retiring them, but neither closes the writer that keeps minting new ones. This is the relationship-kind analogue of the flag lexicon that pm-fs8q9x governs for flags: one concept, one canonical spelling, every historical spelling still accepted as a hidden alias.

The declared dependency-kind domain names exactly one canonical spelling per relation, and every current spelling remains accepted as a hidden alias, proven by a test over the full pre-change spelling set; Write-time canonicalization is uniform: any accepted alias is stored as its canonical kind, extending the single depends_on to blocked_by case shipped under pm-fl0c to the whole domain, so no new alias row can be created; Item type words are no longer accepted as relationship kinds, or the decision to keep them is recorded with the relation each one denotes; pm graph audit and the deps surfaces disclose alias rows still present in stored data as a named legacy count rather than folding them silently into the canonical bucket; The declared canonical set and its alias map are readable from the contracts surface, so a grep or jq pipeline can be written against a documented vocabulary instead of an observed one; Existing alias rows on terminal items are left unmutated; their remediation stays with pm-hnc9w7

value.author: harness:claude-code
value.text:
Direction evidence for the lexicon decision, measured 2026-07-28.

Control established in an isolated sandbox: an item X declaring a dependency row of kind blocks against Y makes X the predecessor of Y — pm graph predecessors Y returns X, pm graph successors X returns Y. The mirrored spelling, Y declaring blocked_by against X, produces the same ordering for the graph engine and additionally reaches the scheduler. Neither write stores a mirror row on the other endpoint, so the two spellings are stored asymmetrically and resolved asymmetrically.

Two consequences for this item's scope, both now filed or recorded rather than remembered.

First, the read side is not merely alias-blind, it is consumer-inconsistent. The graph engine honours blocks; blocker resolution in src/core/item/actionability.ts matches the single literal blocked_by and cannot see it. 219 blocks rows against 127 declared blocked_by rows means the spelling the scheduler ignores is the more common of the two. Owner filed as pm-jkbqt8, blocked on this item because canonicalization is the upstream fix.

Second, the corpus already contains the same kind used in two opposite senses within one item. Every v1-era root declares blocks against pm-doxj, meaning the v1 milestone precedes the roadmap, which is correct. The same items also declare blocks against their own predecessor milestone, meaning Milestone 1 precedes Milestone 0, which is inverted. Twelve such rows across the delivery and PRD chains. This is the concrete instance the direction decision has to rule on, and it is checkable without interpreting prose because the two readings contradict each other inside the same item. Full evidence on pm-1w6scp.

Whatever this item decides, the acceptance test is now available for free: a paired write of both spellings must produce identical predecessor, successor and readiness results, and the twelve inverted legacy rows must land on a stated disposition rather than being silently canonicalized on read while staying wrong on disk.

value.author: harness:claude-code
value.text:
The alias is not legacy. Measured 2026-08-03 over the full corpus by parsing dependency rows structurally rather than through the graph profile.

There are 43 related_to rows. 35 of them sit on items created on or after 2026-07-25, and the newest two were written today. The alias is therefore being minted continuously by current authoring at current HEAD, not inherited from a pre-canonicalization era. The earlier reading that treated a handful of related_to rows as legacy noise on closed holders is superseded by this count.

The reason it stays invisible is the inconsistency this item already owns. related_to canonicalizes on read, so the graph audit profile reports it inside related and edges_by_kind never shows the alias. A maintainer looking at the canonical census sees one associative kind and concludes the vocabulary is settled. Only a structural parse of the stored rows shows two.

This makes the write-time canonicalization criterion the load-bearing one rather than a tidiness item. As long as reads canonicalize and writes do not, the corpus accumulates a second spelling at a measurable rate while every reporting surface asserts that it does not exist, and the divergence is unbounded because nothing can observe it.

The rows themselves stay untouched. All 43 holders are terminal, and rewriting kinds on terminal items churns changelog row ordering for no gain. The fix belongs at the write boundary, after which the stored rows can be normalized once as part of a single deliberate pass rather than opportunistically.
